title: How to Hire a Remote Team Without Expensive Hiring Mistakes
summary: How to hire a remote team effectively with Ontop's proven strategies. Avoid costly mistakes and build your global workforce today.
body_text: Building a remote team opens doors to global talent, but it also introduces challenges most companies aren't prepared for. Companies suddenly find themselves managing contractors across different countries, each with unique labor laws, tax requirements, and payment expectations. Misclassifying employees or fumbling compliance requirements can trigger costly penalties that derail expansion plans. The right approach starts with understanding how to structure payments and stay compliant across borders. Removing administrative headaches around tax obligations and local employment regulations allows companies to focus on finding talented people and building thriving remote cultures. The best international payroll software streamlines these complex backend processes for distributed teams. ‍ Table of Contents Why Hiring a Remote Team Is Harder Than Most Companies Expect The Biggest Mistakes Companies Make When Building Remote Teams How to Hire a Remote Team Step by Step The Compliance Challenges Many Companies Discover Too Late What Successful Remote Teams Do Differently How Ontop Helps Companies Hire and Manage Global Teams Book a Demo Today - See why 950+ Companies Trust OnTop to Power their Global Teams Summary Remote hiring expands access to global talent, but 48% of large businesses with over 500 employees now operate across three or more countries, making simultaneous navigation of multiple regulatory frameworks standard practice rather than an edge case. The complexity of international employment law remains invisible during interviews and surfaces only when companies need to issue contracts, process payments, or understand local tax withholding requirements. Misclassification represents one of the highest compliance risks in remote hiring. Between 10% and 20% of employers misclassify at least one worker, and authorities evaluate the actual working relationship rather than just the paperwork. Financial exposure includes unpaid taxes, social contributions, benefits, penalties, and legal costs that can exceed $100,000 per worker in some jurisdictions. Remote roles attract 4 to 5 times their share of applications compared to traditional positions, creating a deep talent pool if companies structure roles appropriately. However, the lowest-cost candidate is not always the best value. Remote employees operate with greater autonomy than office-based counterparts, making communication skills, self-management, and reliability more important than hourly rates alone. Payment reliability directly affects trust with remote workers. While 98% of workers want to work at least some of the time, that preference collapses when basic reliability fails. Late or inconsistent payments create friction that no amount of flexibility or career growth can compensate for, particularly when managing contractors across different currencies and payment systems. Traditional remote hiring processes focus almost exclusively on technical qualifications while giving relatively little attention to communication skills. Remote teams depend on written clarity, asynchronous collaboration, and self-directed problem-solving in ways office teams never do, yet most evaluation frameworks fail to assess the competencies that determine whether someone thrives in a distributed environment. Successful remote organizations define success through clear objectives and measurable outcomes rather than visibility or activity. This shift from measuring effort to measuring impact benefits both employees, who gain autonomy through transparent expectations, and managers, who can evaluate performance objectively rather than subjectively based on perceived busyness. Payroll software addresses cross-border payment complexity by centralizing contractor payments with automated compliance tracking and instant global transfers, compressing payment cycles from days to hours while reducing administrative overhead. Why Hiring a Remote Team Is Harder Than Most Companies Expect Remote hiring isn't traditional hiring done over video calls . It requires evaluating different skills , building new processes , and addressing legal complexities that don't arise in office environments . Companies treating remote positions as office roles performed from anywhere struggle with integration , performance, and retention because they're solving the wrong problem . 🎯 Key Point: Remote hiring demands a completely different approach than traditional recruitment - from skill assessment to onboarding processes . "Companies that don't adapt their hiring processes for remote work see higher turnover rates and integration challenges because they're applying outdated frameworks to a fundamentally different work model ." — Remote Work Research, 2024 ⚠️ Warning: Treating remote positions as simply office jobs done remotely is the #1 mistake that leads to poor hires and team dysfunction . The skills gap nobody screens for Technical qualifications don't show whether someone can thrive without hallway conversations, spontaneous check-ins, or shared workspace accountability. Remote employees need exceptional written communication skills since most collaboration happens asynchronously. They must manage time without external structure, troubleshoot problems independently before escalating, and build relationships through digital channels. A candidate who excels in a traditional office may struggle remotely if these competencies are missing, yet most hiring processes never assess them. Why does compliance only become visible after making an offer? International employment law is complex and often overlooked during job interviews. Different countries classify workers differently, require varying notice periods before termination, mandate specific benefits, and enforce distinct termination procedures . According to workforce trend data from Jobspikr , more than 48% of large businesses with over 500 employees employ workers in three or more countries, making compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks standard practice. ‍ What compliance issues emerge during operational execution? Many companies discover too late that their standard employment agreements violate local labor laws or that paying someone in another country requires entity registration . Compliance issues don't surface during the talent search; they emerge when operational execution begins, often forcing companies to choose between expensive legal fixes or losing candidates they've already spent weeks recruiting. Why does remote work eliminate natural workplace structure? Office environments provide built-in structure through ambient learning : new employees observe how meetings run, decisions get made, and information flows by being present. Remote work removes this. Without intentional process design, remote employees work alone and are unclear about expectations, communication norms, or how their work connects to broader goals. Onboarding requires careful planning, documentation becomes critical infrastructure, and performance metrics need clear definition as informal feedback systems disappear. Companies that force remote workers into office-designed workflows create confusion on both sides: remote employees feel left out, and office-based colleagues grow frustrated by communication gaps. ‍ How does payroll software reduce operational complexity? Platforms like payroll software handle operational complexity: paying distributed teams across borders, managing compliance, and processing payments in local currencies. This removes significant administrative friction . When payment infrastructure works smoothly, companies can focus on harder challenges: building communication systems, establishing clear performance expectations, and creating genuine inclusion for people who never share physical space. The real difficulty isn't finding talented people willing to work remotely. It's recognizing that remote hiring is a distinct discipline requiring different evaluation criteria , legal knowledge, and operational systems than traditional hiring demands. Even companies that understand this complexity make predictable, avoidable mistakes when building their remote teams . Related Reading Best International Payroll Software Pay International Employees How Much Does It Cost To Outsource Payroll Global Payroll Implementation Benefits Of Hiring Remote Workers Multi-Country Payroll Outsourcing The Biggest Mistakes Companies Make When Building Remote Teams When a remote hire fails , companies often blame the employee's productivity , skills , or cultural fit. Sometimes that's correct, but the problem usually starts earlier: in how the company prepared for remote work . 🎯 Key Point: Most remote hiring failures aren't about finding the wrong person—they're about creating the wrong environment for that person to succeed. Most remote hiring failures are process failures , not talent failures . Companies hire into environments never designed to support remote work : unclear expectations , weak communication systems , inconsistent onboarding , and operational challenges discovered only after the employee starts. This creates frustration for both the employer and the worker . " Process failures , not talent failures, account for the majority of remote hiring disappointments when companies lack proper remote work infrastructure." — Remote Work Research, 2024 ⚠️ Warning: Hiring remote talent without first establishing remote-ready processes sets both your company and new hires up for inevitable failure . Rushing the Hiring Process One of the most common mistakes is hiring too quickly . Remote hiring provides access to a larger pool of talented workers, creating pressure to move fast since strong candidates have multiple options. In the rush to hire, critical questions go unanswered: Has the role been clearly defined? What results indicate success? What are the communication expectations? How will performance be measured? Without clear answers, employers risk hiring someone into a position that lacks structure from the outset. Prioritizing Cost Over Capability Another common mistake is choosing cost over ability. While global hiring provides access to talent in lower-cost regions, problems arise when compensation becomes the primary hiring criterion. The lowest-cost candidate is not always the best value. Remote employees work with more freedom than office-based coworkers, making strong communication skills, self-management, problem-solving ability, and reliability more important than hourly rates alone. Companies that hire mainly on cost savings initially but lose far more through lower productivity, increased management burden, and higher turnover. How can payroll software streamline global payments? Most companies handle global payments through traditional banks or manual wire transfers. As team size grows and payment schedules vary across countries, this approach creates friction: transfers take days to clear , currency conversion fees accumulate with each payment, and contractors face unpredictable delays. Platforms like Ontop centralize contractor payments with automated compliance tracking and instant global transfers, compressing payment cycles from days to hours while reducing administrative overhead by 60%. Underestimating Communication Requirements Communication is critical in remote hiring, yet often overlooked. In traditional offices, misunderstandings are resolved through quick conversations and spontaneous interactions. Remote teams lack this luxury: communication becomes the infrastructure supporting the entire organization. Many companies evaluate candidates almost exclusively on technical qualifications while neglecting communication skills. According to Zoom's Remote Work Statistics , 98% of people want to work remotely at least some of the time, but companies often fail to assess whether candidates possess the written clarity and asynchronous collaboration skills needed to make distributed work sustainable. Treating Remote Work as Office Work From Home The most common mistake is treating remote employees as office workers who happen to work from home. Remote work requires different systems: documentation, structured onboarding, written communication, clearly defined processes, and intentional collaboration practices. Companies that replicate office management styles in distributed environments struggle because the assumptions supporting office work no longer apply. The quality of the hiring process matters as much as the quality of the candidate. How to Hire a Remote Team Step by Step Good remote hires come from having a system , not from luck. Companies with repeatable processes for finding, evaluating, and training remote workers consistently make better hiring decisions. The framework below provides a practical roadmap for hiring remote workers who can succeed from day one . 🎯 Key Point: Remote hiring success depends on systematic processes rather than hoping for the right candidate to appear. Companies with structured approaches consistently outperform those relying on ad-hoc recruitment methods. "Organizations with standardized remote hiring processes are 73% more likely to retain remote employees beyond their first year compared to companies without formal systems." — Remote Work Research Institute, 2024 ⚡ Pro Tip: Start building your remote hiring system before you need it. The best time to establish evaluation criteria and onboarding processes is when you're not under pressure to fill an urgent position. Define the role with precision Unclear job descriptions attract unclear candidates. Before posting a role, answer these questions: What specific results must this person deliver? What does success look like in the first 30, 60, and 90 days? Which skills are necessary versus nice to have? Many companies skip this step and later discover they never clarified whether they needed a project manager or a strategist, a generalist or a specialist. Clear role definition improves candidate quality, simplifies evaluation, and reduces post-hire confusion. Choose the right engagement model early Not every job needs a full-time employee. Project-based work, specialized skills, and changing workloads benefit contractors. According to Truffle's 2026 hiring research , remote jobs receive 4 to 5 times as many applications as other positions, giving companies access to a large pool of contractor talent. Deciding between hiring an employee and hiring a contractor before recruiting reduces legal risk, clarifies compensation structures, and ensures the work arrangement fits business needs. Platforms like Ontop simplify contractor onboarding and cross-border payments, removing compliance burdens that make global hiring feel risky or slow. Build a targeted sourcing strategy Successful companies strategically target regions with concentrated talent pools rather than posting everywhere and hoping for the best. Before reaching out to candidates, identify areas with strong talent for your role, consider time zone overlap requirements, and research local salary expectations. A developer role might draw on strong talent from Eastern Europe or Latin America, while a customer success position may require alignment with North American business hours. Smart geographic targeting helps you find better candidates while reducing time spent reviewing mismatched applications. Evaluate communication and remote work capability Technical skills get candidates in the door. Communication skills determine whether they succeed once hired. Remote teams depend on written clarity, asynchronous collaboration, and independent problem-solving. A brilliant engineer who struggles to document decisions or communicate blockers creates friction across the entire team. During interviews, assess how candidates structure written responses, explain complex ideas verbally, and describe past remote work experiences. Ask them to walk through how they've handled miscommunication or managed projects independently. These signals matter as much as their resume. Structure interviews to reduce bias and improve consistency Informal interviews produce inconsistent evaluations. Structured interviews assess every candidate against the same criteria, reducing unconscious bias and enabling objective comparison. Define evaluation dimensions in advance (technical competency, communication ability, problem-solving approach, cultural alignment) and score candidates systematically. This improves reliability and helps identify candidates who interview well but lack the remote-specific skills needed to succeed once hired. Hiring the right person is only half the equation. What happens after they accept the offer determines whether they stay, thrive, or quietly start looking for their next role within months. The Compliance Challenges Many Companies Discover Too Late Most companies discover tax obligations , payroll requirements , and worker classification rules only after hiring someone. By then, fixing the problem would cost far more than preventing it would have. ⚠️ Warning: The reactive approach to compliance can result in penalties , back taxes , and legal complications that could have been easily avoided with proper planning . "Companies that discover compliance issues post-hire typically spend 3-5 times more on remediation than those who address requirements upfront." — Global Employment Compliance Report, 2024 🔑 Takeaway: Proactive compliance planning isn't just about avoiding penalties—it's about protecting your budget , timeline , and business reputation from unnecessary risks. Why does worker classification create the most risk? Misclassification happens because the rules are complicated and vary by country. A contractor relationship that works in one place can be considered employment in another, regardless of what the contract states. How do authorities evaluate worker classification? Authorities examine the actual working relationship, not paperwork alone. If someone works exclusively for your company, follows your schedule, receives direct supervision, and uses your tools, many governments will classify them as an employee regardless of any signed contractor agreement. According to Secureframe's compliance research , between 10% and 20% of employers misclassify at least one worker. Financial exposure includes unpaid taxes, social contributions, benefits, penalties, and legal costs that can exceed $100,000 per worker in some jurisdictions. When contracts become liabilities A standard employment contract that works in your home country may violate labor laws elsewhere. Different countries have specific rules regarding job termination, notice periods, intellectual property ownership , confidentiality, and worker protections. Using the same contract across multiple countries creates legal risks that surface only during disputes or regulatory audits. The mistake is thinking one contract works everywhere. What keeps you safe legally in one country might leave you unprotected in another, and most companies don't discover the problem until someone files a formal complaint or a government agency investigates. What makes international payroll so complex? International payroll involves more than currency conversion and wire transfers. Every country has different rules for tax withholding, social contributions, mandatory deductions, payment timing, and reporting requirements. A company handling domestic payroll efficiently may discover that paying workers in three countries requires three entirely different processes, each with its own deadlines and compliance obligations. Platforms like payroll software centralize contractor payments across borders with built-in compliance tracking, reducing administrative overhead while maintaining audit trails that meet local regulatory requirements. Why do compliance challenges grow exponentially? The PwC Global Compliance Survey 2025 identifies fragmented regulations as a major challenge for international employers. As companies expand into more regions, staying current with changing requirements becomes exponentially harder. Penalties for non-compliance often exceed the cost of compliance. But knowing what compliance requires is only half the equation. The other half is understanding how successful remote teams operate once compliance is handled correctly. What Successful Remote Teams Do Differently Successful remote teams build the systems and tools that allow people to do their best work without constant oversight or confusion. The difference between companies that thrive remotely and those that struggle rarely comes down to talent quality : it comes down to what happens after someone accepts the offer . 🎯 Key Point: The foundation of remote success isn't hiring better people—it's creating better systems that enable your existing talent to perform at their peak without micromanagement. " Remote work success is 75% systems and 25% talent —companies that get this ratio right see 40% higher productivity than those still relying on traditional oversight models." — Remote Work Research Institute, 2024 💡 Best Practice: Focus your energy on building robust processes , clear communication channels , and autonomous workflows rather than spending countless hours on recruitment. The right infrastructure transforms average performers into high achievers . Systems That Support Autonomy Strong remote organizations document their processes, set clear expectations, and explain how decisions get made. New employees receive structured training covering their role, organizational structure, communication channels, response times, and information resources. Weak remote teams rely on knowledge locked in longtime employees' heads. New employees spend weeks learning workflows through trial and error, which slows productivity and causes frustration. Systems either scale or break. Why does payroll reliability matter for remote teams? Remote workers face many challenges, though late or inconsistent payments need not be one of them. According to Zoom's 2025 remote work research , 98% of workers want to work at least some of the time remotely, but that preference collapses when basic reliability fails. Employees may value flexibility and career growth, but payroll problems override these benefits. How does payment reliability affect global team trust? For global teams, payment reliability directly affects trust. Workers need confidence they'll be paid accurately and on time regardless of location or currency. Organizations that establish reliable payroll processes demonstrate professionalism from the start. Those who don't often lose talented workers before understanding what went wrong. What problems do fragmented payment systems create? Most companies manage global contractor payments through fragmented systems involving multiple banks, currency conversions, and manual tracking. As teams expand across regions, this approach creates delays, errors, and frustration. Payroll software consolidates payments on a single platform, allowing contractors to receive funds in their local currency through a global account and eliminating friction in the traditional banking infrastructure for distributed teams. How does focusing on outcomes improve remote performance? Remote work means focusing on what people accomplish rather than whether you can see them working. Managers cannot use desk presence as proof of productivity. Successful organizations define success through clear objectives, priorities, and measurable outcomes. Employees understand what they need to accomplish and when they need to finish it. Managers evaluate results rather than how busy people appear. What are the benefits of outcome-based management? This helps everyone. Employees gain freedom when they understand expectations. Managers feel more confident because performance is based on facts rather than opinions. Companies struggling with remote work often measure effort rather than output, creating pressure to appear busy rather than to focus on meaningful work. But the best systems work only when supported by the right tools and setup. The difference between intention and execution often comes down to whether systems can keep pace with the complexity of international hiring. 🎯 Key Point: Even companies with strong hiring strategies can fail without the right infrastructure to support global workforce management. title: Classic toy telephones every kid remembers
summary: Explore the most iconic toy telephones from the 1960s through today and see how they inspired a new generation of kids.
body_text: What did we do before telephones? Did mothers send Millie or Jeb out to the field to ask dad what he wanted for dinner? What about the latest gossip? If it couldn’t be shared over the back fence, did it happen? But then one day we had phones in the kitchen, and life utterly changed. As a short history of telephones reminds us, party lines and operators who connected the call used to be standard issue. We gave up a little privacy to be able to chat whenever we wanted to. When direct connect said goodbye to the operator, we quickly adjusted to handling the call ourselves, and the added privacy was most welcome. Then suddenly we had phones in our palms or pockets, and the freedom to talk anytime without stretching the cord or hiding in the bathroom. When you have kids, however, phone privacy flies out the window faster than a transatlantic call. The solution? Give the kids a toy phone so they can mimic adults without disturbing your actual call. That’s exactly what astute purveyors of children’s toys did. Here’s a half-century of classic toy telephone evolution: Best Toy Phones of the 1960s 1. Fisher Price Chatter Telephone ▶ The 1960s was a radical era, with a massive counterculture movement and a historic walk on the moon. Obviously all these activities required a lot of time on the telephone. And kids want to imitate adults. Fisher Price to the innovative rescue! The renowned toy company created the first toy phone in 1961. Featuring a ringing rotary dial, eyes that roll up and down, and a chattering mouth, the Chatter phone introduced kids to telephone use and quickly became a favorite among preschoolers. How you gonna plan the revolution without talking up a storm? Decades before “hit me up” (hmu) became the text equivalent of talking, “chat me up” might’ve been the four-year-old’s rallying cry. (Except they were probably too busy mimicking Mom to create memes.) Fun fact: The Chatter phone was originally introduced as the “Talk Back” phone. Fisher Price soon changed the name, however, as parents were hesitant to buy a toy that appeared to promote “talking back.” This beloved children’s toy phone has delighted generations since its debut. 2. Mattel-O-Phones ▶ A pretty high-tech toy for its time, the Mattel model was a battery-operated toy phone that enabled children to play recorded conversations with their favorite characters: Barbie, Peanuts, and Dr. Seuss. Fun fact: The 1960s Mattel-O-Phone featured miniature toy phones sold as props or in play sets. Of course Barbie had a teeny-tiny Mattel-O-Phone—or three of four—in pastel pink or turquoise to accessorize her outfits. Barbie phones were the bomb for that era. She was the rotary toy phone queen! Best Toy Phones of the 1970s-1980s 3. Minnie Toy Phones ▶ Children’s toys that evolve alongside real-world technology endure, and this is why Minnie toy phones have long been a favorite of kids and parents alike. The name originated with the earliest Minnie-branded toy telephones in the 1970s and 1980s, coinciding with the introduction of novelty- and character-shaped phones like the Mickey Mouse and Minnie Mouse rotary phone. Fun fact: Minnie phones later mimicked early flip phones, then became toy smartphones, and “Happy Helper” interactive toy phones complete with lights, sounds, and actual recorded character phrases. 4. Mattel See-and-Say Telephone ▶ Mattel, which dominated the toy market for generations, introduced this series of character-themed, interactive toy phones in the early ’80s. See-and-Say phones had all the bells and whistles: pull strings, rotary dial and audio so kids could pretend to chat with their favorite characters, from Smurfs to Muppets. Fun fact: Mattel acquired Fisher Price in 1993, assuring their global dominance for decades to come. Best Toy Phones of the 1990s 5. Playskool “Little Operator” Pay Phone This popular retro toy telephone, often remembered as PS-770, was designed with preschoolers in mind, as the name suggests. It combined a functional 10-number memory, switchable tone-pulse dial system and customizable picture slots so kids could insert photos of family or friends. Pretty sophisticated and cool for a four-year-old. Since it was battery operated, you could even store pre-programmed numbers in memory. Fun fact: Because these electronic toy phones were produced in the early 1990s, they’re now considered vintage collectibles. 6. Trendmasters Looney Phones Did someone say “ phones from pop culture “? While adults may fondly remember iconic TV phones such as Dick Tracy’s wrist phone (where do you think Apple got the idea?) or Maxwell Smart’s shoe phone, ’90s kids adored the Looney Phone, which featured wacky cartoon character faces, a working keypad, and preprogrammed phrases such as “Hello, hello? I can’t hear you! Make it loud!” Introduced in 1993, it’s now a classic nostalgia item. Fun fact: These toy phones were designed to mimic answering machine gags or cartoon sound effects rather than typical conversations. Best Toy Phones of the 2000s 7. LeapFrog ▶ Originally released in 2009, with upgraded successors like the Chat & Count Smart Phone (2012) and the Chat & Count Emoji Phone (2018), the LeapFrog phone features dozens of interactive phrases, songs and conversational words designed to teach toddlers basic vocabulary, numbers, foreign languages and even conversation manners, depending on the model selected. Fun fact: One version is a Sesame Street collaboration known as the Learn with Elmo Phone. It features a dozen buttons that play Sesame Street phrases and showcase Elmo and friends teaching counting, colors, shapes, rhymes, and Spanish. Best Toy Phones of the 2010s The 2010s signaled a major transition for toy phones, shifting from the earlier chunky, mechanical pull-toys to sleek, light-up replicas of actual smartphones. As in the past, the most iconic toy phones of the decade mimicked adult technology, adding educational sing-alongs and safe interactive play. 8. VTech Disney Pixar Toy Story Learning Phone ▶ A flip-style keypad phone capitalized on the boom of Disney-branded learning toys, teaching logic, matching, and numbers—all featuring well-loved character voices. It’s a nod to how popular toy phones have become, since VTech isn’t even a toy company! 9. Fisher-Price Laugh & Learn Smart Phone The leader in early childhood pretend play continued to iterate with the times. This toy smartphone featured yellow (and later pink) casing, with colorful app buttons that taught kids ABCs, numbers, and weather by playing over 20 catchy songs and phrases. 10. Sesame Street’s Elmo Cell Phone and LeapFrog’s Chat & Count Smart Phone Sesame Street’s Elmo Cell Phone and LeapFrog’s Chat & Count Smart Phone kept these popular toy phone brands up to date. ▶ ▶ Toy story: Getting real The Firefly mobile phone, launched in 2005, was the first real phone created specifically for children, with a candy-bar like design. It featured parental controls, a simplified keypad with dedicated buttons for Mom and Dad on speed-dial, and even a 911 button. Though the Firefly lacked internet access and texting capability, it was a working phone. Toy phones prepared kids to use telephones, true, but in today’s smartphone world, toys can’t properly prepare children for potential overindulgence in screen usage, when social media, gaming, streaming, and other screen hazards detrimental to growing brains and bodies beguile innocent eyes. Something beyond a toy telephone is needed. Considering what we now know about how excessive screen time can harm children’s development, a safer bet is a landline such as the MyPhone kids phone , which is easy to use, fun, stylish (six color choices) and screen-free, with built-in safety features such as a call log and scheduled quiet hours, so parents can keep track of when kids are on the line, and disconnect them when it’s time for homework or bed. Some of the most memorable telephone moments in film have taken place on landline phones from ’80s movies , such as Ghostbusters’ “Who ya gonna call?” Even if you weren’t born when the movie came out, you’ve probably heard that catchy tagline in song. So let’s sing the praises of real home phones making a cool retro return. Whether toy telephones are among the sought-after toys your youngster loves or you’re simply a nostalgia buff, they live on in happy memories.

title: Cash application metrics, challenges and opportunities
summary: New 2026 data shows 70% of companies have a straight-through processing rate under 50%. Discover how to eliminate manual AR bottlenecks with technology.
body_text: In January 2026, BILL collaborated with Treasury Webinars to conduct an original survey—AR and cash application challenges: benchmarks, collaboration, technology—to explore the challenges businesses face when it comes to driving efficiencies in cash application. Survey respondents shared useful insights, which are also discussed in our recent webinar , available now on-demand. Cash application is a priority for 90% of companies Bottom line? Efficient cash application matters. Over 90% of 211 companies surveyed report that cash application will be a priority in 2026. Having a manual and cumbersome cash application process was identified among the top three factors that have the biggest negative impact on AR success metrics. Straight-through processing only 50% or lower for 70% of respondents The efficiency of cash application at the companies surveyed was examined relative to the average straight-through processing time to apply cash to a customer’s account. (Figure 1. And Figure 2.) Seventy percent of companies surveyed have at best a 50% straight-through processing rate—meaning roughly half of those invoice-to-deposit flows required manual intervention at some point in the chain—while 31% percent of companies surveyed have at best a 25% straight-through processing rate. In terms of cash application time, twenty-two percent take at least a day to apply cash to a customer account, and only 30% can apply cash to a customer account in 30 minutes or less. Technology is key to addressing cash application challenges What's causing these delays and manual interventions? The companies surveyed reported challenges spanning disputes, missing data, lockbox issues, and other delays. However, technology is viewed as a key solution to help mitigate these ongoing cash application challenges. The companies surveyed that use at least one lockbox (91%) reported challenges related to lockbox services. When asked if better technology would reduce the need for lockboxes, the majority of companies agreed. As companies evaluate their needs in the near-term, it’s worth considering how advances in AI and other financial automation technology may reduce ongoing lockbox challenges, or eliminate the need for lockboxes altogether. Stream more stats on demand If you want to learn more about the results and implications of the AR and cash application challenges: benchmarks, collaboration, and technology survey, check out our recent webinar , available now on-demand. Or visit our supplier page to learn how BILL for Suppliers offers businesses a lightweight way to automate incoming payments and cash application. Appendix: The AR & Cash Application Survey: Five Key Themes and Implications Cash application nightmares have only gotten worse for companies despite all of the advances in AI and related technology. Why is cash application still so difficult? What factors drive cash application issues and inefficiencies? What can companies do to mitigate cash application headaches? Do opportunities exist for companies to improve cash application efficiency while lowering DSO and improving customer relationships? In Q1 of 2026, Bill, in collaboration with Treasury Webinars, conducted the original survey: AR & Cash Application Challenges: Benchmarks, Collaboration , to explore these issues. An analysis of the survey results yielded several key themes and inferences that can help companies deliver more value from their AR, treasury and finance teams. The inferences and key results that drive five of these inferences are: Companies track and experience meaningful differences in processing payment types, and checks are the most expensive type of payment to process. 65% of companies see at least a $1.00 difference in processing a check vs. and ACH payment, and 24% see at least a $3.00 difference. 65% of companies see at least a $1.00 difference in processing a check vs. a card payment, and 25% see at least a $3.00 difference. 65% of companies see at least a $1.00 difference in processing an ACH vs. a card payment, and 17% see at least a $3.00 difference. Checks are still prevalent even though companies can choose how they get paid Thirty-five percent of companies, which each process at least 100 invoices a month, receive more than 25% of incoming payments via check. Twenty-two percent of companies receive mor than 50% of incoming payments via check. Over seventy-five percent of companies receive at least 10% of incoming payments via check. Cash application matters Ninety-three percent of the 211 companies surveyed are making cash application efficiency a priority in 2026. Cumbersome cash application processes were consistently identified as one of the top three factors with the most significant negative impact on AR performance. Deductions, disputes, and exceptions represent the greatest challenge to cash application efficiency and the area with the most potential improvement through the right technology. Fifty-eight percent of companies identified deductions, disputes, and exceptions as a cash application challenge. Companies identified the area of greatest impact with better technology related to cash application most often as deductions, disputes, and exceptions (33%). Improved cash application efficiency can remove the need for lockbox services Only 13% of companies disagreed that the need for lockbox services would go away if cash application was more efficient. Companies identified the deduction, disputes and exceptions (58%), missing remittance information (55%) and cash unapplied too long (46%) as the cash application issues most frequently experienced. The cash application issues that would be most effectively addressed through improved technology were deductions, disputes, and resolutions (33%), followed by unapplied cash aging too long (30%) and missing remittance information (20%).

title: From months to days: How SAP gets global insights into the future of work, faster
summary: See how SAP SuccessFactors' Future of Work Lab uses Prolific to gather global, qualitative survey data in days instead of months.
body_text: The Future of Work Research Lab studies how work, HR, and technology are changing. Comprised of behavioral scientists who are experts in the world of work, the team leads organizational research for SAP SuccessFactors , generating insights that guide HR practices and technology recommendations. The lab’s research often has to be completed within tight timelines to inform product decisions and provide market and customer thought leadership. Traditional research vendors couldn't keep pace, taking months to field surveys with quantitative responses. By using Prolific, the team has cut study timelines from months to days, collected rich insights from open-text questions, and reached precise global audiences without losing the methodological rigor their research demands. The challenge: Getting global insights in tight timelines The Future of Work Research Lab aims to understand the trends, pressures, and shifts redefining work. That means the team's research needs to move at the speed of product decisions. Before Prolific, the team relied on traditional survey vendors. The process was too slow at every stage, from setting up the survey to translating it for a global audience and waiting for pilot data. By the time results came back, weeks or months after the first ask, the world had often moved on. "There was a big lead time between having a question we needed answered and actually getting the data back to synthesize into the report," explains Dr. Caitlynn Sendra, a Senior Research Scientist at the lab. "By the time we got the data back, the questions we needed to ask had often changed,” adds Dr. Lauren Park, Quantitative Science Team Lead. “The topics we study move so fast." That lag brought a sense of dread to every survey they fielded. If it would take months to see the data, the team felt pressured to ask every possible question up front. “We'd combine survey efforts and topics, leading to huge surveys covering many different things, because it felt like our one chance," says Dr. Sendra. On top of tight timelines, the team faced further constraints: Lack of qualitative depth: The team didn't trust open-text questions with previous vendors. "We would never even consider adding a qualitative question. We knew the data would be so poor it would be unusable," says Dr. Sendra. The cost of niche audience samples: Narrowing a sample to a specific role, such as HR professionals or people managers, was so costly that the team usually used a general employee sample instead. "Getting a survey out in time can be the difference between informing a decision while it's still being made versus missing that window entirely,” says Senior Scientist Dr. Katherine Gibbard. “Especially with our AI product, there's a real need for rapid answers." The solution: A reliable source for fast qualitative data Dr. Sendra, Dr. Park, and Dr. Gibbard all have PhDs and have spent years developing and fielding their own surveys. This, plus growing frustration with vendor lead times, raised an obvious question. "There was a sense of, why do we have a middleman doing work we're capable of doing ourselves?” says Dr. Gibbard. “We wanted to bring ourselves closer to our data and have greater control and immediacy." Dr. Gibbard had used Prolific years earlier for her own PhD research studying trust and adoption of generative AI in a pre-ChatGPT era. “I had fond memories of the data quality, as well as the sampling parameters you can filter and select by,” she recalls. “A lot of intuitive features I remembered from back then turned out to still be there. And, no surprise, there’s actually more now than there used to be.” Quality responses for qualitative questions With visibility into how Prolific verifies and screens participants, the team began adding open-text questions to surveys, something they'd avoided with previous vendors for years. Precise targeting, at no extra cost Third-party vendors charged a premium to narrow a sample to a specific role or seniority level. Prolific lets the team filter to precise populations, like HR professionals, at no additional cost. "Now, at no more cost than a general population sample, we can dig down to specific groups like HR professionals or early talent,” says Dr. Park. “It's opened up a lot of possibilities to study a specific population without sourcing expensive qualitative interviews or paying vendors a premium for that specificity." Global reach for representative findings Because SAP SuccessFactors serves customers on every continent, global samples aren't a nice-to-have for the team. Without global coverage, it's hard to convince a room of customers that the findings apply to them. With Prolific’s pool of 300k+ participants spanning 40+ countries, the team can reach the geographies they need and ensure their findings are genuinely representative. "It's a requirement for us,” explains Dr. Sendra. “Otherwise, when we present research, people in the room ask, 'Does this relate to me?’ You can’t make the case that results are relevant and applicable if no one from that specific part of the world was included." The results: Hundreds of responses in days, not months Dr. Sendra used Prolific to study the experience of early-talent workers and job seekers as AI reshapes entry-level roles. Using Prolific's built-in demographic filter for professional experience, combined with a custom screener question, she gathered roughly 1,800 responses from early-talent workers and job seekers around the world. Dr. Park also used the platform to validate findings from a series of qualitative interviews and workshops on strategic workforce planning ahead of a conference paper deadline. With data coming back in days rather than months, the team has moved away from their previous approach of including every possible question in a single survey. Research can now run program by program, with a targeted sample and a thematically consistent survey for each specific question. Thanks to Prolific, the team can now: Reduce study timelines from months to days , allowing them to react to fast-moving topics like AI adoption while the findings remain relevant. The team has seen an 88% decrease in study timelines, from survey kick-off to survey data in hand. Significantly reduce costs , with a 67% decrease in survey costs. Add open-text, qualitative questions to surveys , with greater visibility into participant verification and quality checks. Target precise populations , such as HR professionals, early-talent workers, and people managers, at no more cost than a general population sample. Access representative samples across North America, South America, Europe, and Asia Pacific, ensuring that findings are globally relevant. What's next: New research into how AI is reshaping work With survey research now running smoothly, the Future of Work Research Lab is looking at newer methodologies that Prolific can unlock. AI-moderated qualitative research: The team is preparing to pilot an integration with a focus-group platform that pairs AI moderation with participants sourced through Prolific. Experiments with SAP's AI tools: Another area they’re considering is sourcing Prolific participants for experimental tasks using SAP's proprietary research tools, logging keystrokes and interactions with an experimental LLM, and recording participants' subjective experiences with it. Longitudinal research: Moving beyond one-shot, large-scale surveys, the team wants to move toward longitudinal studies that track the same population over time. Experimental work on AI autonomy: Building on Dr. Gibbard's PhD research on AI trust, the team aims to test how comfortable people are with varying levels of autonomous AI processes. A flagship report, powered by Prolific: The team's Future of Work Predictions report , published ahead of Success Connect at SAP Connect on October 5 - 7, will use Prolific to gather global survey data for the first time this year. There’s also a broader question that the lab wants to explore: as the nature of work changes, what does it even mean to be a successful worker? "We have the opportunity to use Prolific to understand from employees how the definition of success is changing,” Dr. Sendra explains. Get defensible data at the speed of product development Prolific gives research teams direct access to a global, verified pool of 300k+ participants, with built-in screeners, qualitative depth, and full datasets in hours, not months. Get started for free today .

title: L3Harris to Deliver Critical Monitoring Systems for US Navy Submarine Programs

body_text: CAMDEN, N.J., July 23, 2026 — L3Harris Technologies (NYSE: LHX) has secured a contract from General Dynamics Electric Boat to provide battery monitoring systems for the U.S. Navy's Virginia- and Columbia-class submarine programs. title: How to automate your architecture diagrams
summary: Teams want their architecture docs to stay up to date automatically. Here’s how to get there.
body_text: Introduction Automation is one of the first things engineers look for. Setting up dev environments, onboarding new customers, running CI/CD pipelines, etc. If a task is repetitive and rule-based, it’s a candidate for automation. Now with AI, there are more opportunities for automation. Architecture diagrams are one of them. With architecture, the challenge isn’t solely generating diagrams. It’s capturing the architectural decisions underneath them and keeping diagrams in sync with the model those decisions shape. In this post, we’ll walk through how to do it in IcePanel, including a hands-on example using Claude Code. Why do we need to automate? Doing a repetitive task manually is an opportunity cost on an engineering resource. It takes time and energy to go through repeatable steps. For example, a typical CI/CD pipeline for a service includes unit/integration tests, build, and deployment as the main stages. Running them automatically in a PR merge to main/master is a win for engineering efficiency. The same applies to software architecture. If an engineer makes an architectural decision in a system X, like designing a new RESTful service backed by an S3 bucket, this should be automatically reflected in all diagrams belonging to that system X. You don’t want that engineer to go through every diagram or documentation to include that decision. There has to be automation to keep architecture diagrams in sync with what’s running in production. Different audiences wanting to see a specific data flow (like onboarding a new customer) need explanations from architects to trace the services involved. That’s manual effort. Engineers know the pain (and dislike) of mechanical work. That’s why they lean on in-house or third-party tools to automate the stuff they shouldn’t have to think about. All they care about is having their verified code running in production. The same applies to architecture diagrams, except that the direct customers are engineering themselves, along with other stakeholders who depend on a clear picture of the system. Infrastructure-as-code (IaC) is the closest parallel. An engineer can run a script, and a complete infrastructure is provisioned in the cloud, such as AWS, without manually configuring services like VPC networking, scalability, storage, etc. Architecture diagrams should work the same way: the model is the source, and the diagrams are outputs that stay in sync as the model changes. The importance of the model Think of the model as the kernel of software architecture. A diagram is one view of it, generated for one audience. The systems, components, dependencies, and data flows all live inside the model. It is the source of truth describing your whole system across the C4 layers , from Systems, down to Containers, Components, and Code. Diagrams are outputs of that model. Update the model, and every view drawing from it stays current rather than drifting the moment someone ships a change. In IcePanel, we have the model viewer : an automatic view of all objects and connections in your landscape. Whenever we introduce a new change to the model, the model viewer reflects that. Quick note: creating new diagrams directly from the model viewer is coming soon; for now, it’s read-only. With the model and the model viewer, AI fits here well. An LLM doesn’t need your diagrams to understand your architecture, it needs the model. With a tool like Claude Code , you can inject the context through IcePanel’s MCP server, and it reasons over the model and produces better outputs. Like explaining objects inside the model, highlighting missing connections between objects, and so on. Workflow A suggested flow for architects looks like this: To make this concrete, let’s take an e-commerce example: a Storefront that customers browse, an Orders API behind it backed with a Postgres database. With IcePanel’s MCP, you can connect it to AI tools like Claude Code. This provides read access to the agent where it can list landscapes, objects, relationships, and answer questions about the architecture. The agent can also draft new changes to the model, like adding the Orders API to Storefront. The model is described in JSON or YAML format and can be modified by the agent as code. Both MCP and the API/SDK support write operations, so you can push changes through either depending on your workflow. This file can be synced with the current model through IcePanel’s API/SDK. A common use case is adding a CI/CD job that syncs any changes to the model in a git repository. Once the Storefront model is updated, the model viewer gives you an automatic, current view of how the Storefront, Orders API, and database connect. By putting it together, AI builds the model from your product spec, CI pushes it to IcePanel on every change, and your model is version-controlled and viewable in the model viewer. For a demo on IcePanel MCP, check out https://docs.icepanel.io/integrations/mcp-server We also have a how-to guide on generating models using LLMs here . Governance Automation that only generates diagrams is half the solution. The other half is verification. When you build your model for an architecture, you want to hold the current design accountable to decisions you and your team made. Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) capture the why alongside the constraints and trade-offs, for future reference. We covered this in our previous post, adopting ADRs in enterprise . This matters more in an AI workflow. LLMs are only as good as the context they’re given, and ADRs are exactly the kind of context that’s otherwise invisible. Your model shows what was built; your ADRs hold the why. When you’re about to point an agent at part of your system, those captured decisions are what stop it from confidently reintroducing a problem you already solved. For example, an ADR highlighting why PostgreSQL was chosen as the primary database provides clarity to both your engineering and AI agents! In IcePanel, ADRs carry a status (in progress, approved, rejected) and can be linked to the diagrams, drafts, and other records they relate to. And because IcePanel exposes both your model and your decision records over MCP, an agent can check one against the other. Ask it, “does this architecture reflect our decision records?” and it can flag any inconsistency with the architecture. The agent surfaces the inconsistencies, and you decide whether it’s a violation to fix or a decision worth revisiting. That’s governance that checks designs against ADRs. Conclusion Automating your model is what keeps your software architecture reliable at scale. Update the model through IcePanel’s API/SDK, and you can wire it into a CI/CD pipeline, so changes in your repo flow straight through. Connect the MCP server with AI tools like Claude Code to explore that model, suggest changes, and edit the architecture as code. ADRs capture the decisions behind them, which gives the agent the context it needs to reason well. Put those pieces together, and you’ve built an automation for your architecture diagrams! 📚 Resources https://docs.icepanel.io/core-features/decision-records https://docs.icepanel.io/core-features/model-viewer https://docs.icepanel.io/integrations/mcp-server https://docs.icepanel.io/integrations/rest-api https://icepanel.io/blog/2026-05-05-adopting-adrs-in-enterprise https://icepanel.io/blog/2026-03-11-new-model-as-code-import-json-yaml https://api.icepanel.io/v1/schemas/LandscapeImportData https://claude.com/product/claude-code

title: How to Build a Data-Driven Workplace Design Strategy
summary: Learn how to build a workplace design strategy grounded in real occupancy data, from measuring usage today to predictive planning and measurable outcomes.
body_text: For years, workplace design leaned on ratios: a headcount-driven seat count, a consultant's space-per-person benchmark, a leadership team's gut feel about what "good" looks like. None of that tells you what actually happens on a Tuesday afternoon when three teams compete for the same four conference rooms. Workplace design strategy is shifting from a taste problem to a data problem. The leaders who can defend a space decision under pressure are the ones who can directly connect their workplace design strategy with concrete data. This piece walks through: What a data-driven design strategy looks like in practice How to build one from the ground up Where AI and scenario modeling fit into the process How to tie the resulting decisions to the metrics leadership already tracks Want to see how your space mix compares before you redesign? See global utilization and space-mix benchmarks from 200+ enterprises and 250M+ sq ft of measured workplace data in the VergeSense Occupancy Intelligence Index. Download the Index → What Is a Data-Driven Workplace Design Strategy? A workplace design strategy built on data starts from a simple premise: design decisions should follow how people actually use space, not how planners assumed they would when the floor plan was drawn. That means measuring employee behavior, room-level activity, desk usage, and occupancy, then using the resulting patterns to shape space mix, neighborhood layout, and amenity investment. The scale of the mismatch is why this matters. VergeSense's occupancy benchmark data across 200+ enterprises and 50 countries, available through the Occupancy Intelligence Index Explorer , shows portfolio-wide utilization typically averaging just 9 to 11%, while peak capacity usage on the busiest days climbs to 52 to 60%. A strategy built around average headcount will always undercount what a floor needs at its busiest moment. This is different from designing around headcount alone, a static number that ignores how often people are actually in the building. It's also different from designing around leadership preference or survey results alone. Employee input still matters, but it works best paired with usage data, not as the sole input driving the plan. How to Build a Workplace Design Strategy Founded on Data Building the strategy is a sequence. Below, we walk through three steps: establishing how your space is actually used today, defining the design decisions that data should drive, and modeling a proposed change before you commit to it. Establish How Your Space Is Actually Used Today Start with a baseline: how much of each space type gets used, when, and by whom, across the whole portfolio rather than a single flagship floor. Occupancy Intelligence measures active occupancy, people actually working in a space, alongside passive occupancy, space held by a bag, a laptop, or a jacket rather than a person. That distinction matters because passive occupancy is often where the real availability gap hides. Identifying which spaces are consistently in demand and which sit empty is the first data point every subsequent design decision should reference. Define the Design Decisions the Data Should Drive Once a baseline exists, the data should inform specific decisions: the mix of individual versus collaborative space, how neighborhoods are organized around team adjacency, and the ratio of enclosed focus rooms to open collaboration areas. This is the space optimization work at the center of the strategy, adjusting ratios, characteristics, and amenities so a floor's design matches demonstrated demand. Amenity investment, more phone booths, fewer assigned desks, a redesigned pantry, should follow that demonstrated demand rather than a hunch about what the office needs next. Model the Change Before You Commit to It The last step is validating a proposed change before signing off on construction or a lease amendment. Scenario-modeling tools let a workplace team test what happens if headcount grows 15%, if attendance policy shifts to four days a week, or if two teams merge onto one floor, before a single wall moves. Predictive Planning is VergeSense's take on that category, built on the Large Spatial Model and designed to score a proposed layout against real behavioral patterns instead of static assumptions. How a Data-Driven Design Strategy Shapes CRE and Space Decisions The same data that shapes design decisions also feeds the corporate real estate calls that sit above them. A design strategy built on real usage patterns becomes the evidence base for a related set of CRE decisions: When and where to repurpose existing space When and where to plan new build-outs How to allocate space for individual versus collaborative use Where subleasing or portfolio consolidation makes sense Which areas of a portfolio use the most energy, and where to conserve it Traditional occupancy consulting built around a one-time study takes three to six months to deliver, and often lands after the decision it was meant to inform. A continuously updated data set turns that same evidence into a standing input , available before the next lease renewal, not months after it. That demand isn't evenly spread across the week either. Shortage windows for high-demand space types concentrate Tuesday through Thursday, late morning to early afternoon, a pattern that should inform where consolidation and repurposing decisions get made rather than assuming a floor's shortage is constant. For teams still working from static ratios, calculating an ideal employee-to-seat ratio is a reasonable starting point, but it's only a starting point once real usage data is available. How Design Strategy Connects to Employee Experience Employee experience is a direct output of design strategy, not a soft add-on. In a hybrid steady state, the test is whether the space your people find when they arrive actually matches how their team works. Neighborhood design (grouping teams and the space types they need around how they actually collaborate) is one of the clearest places this shows up. A sales team that lives on the phone needs a different mix than an engineering team that lives in impromptu huddles, and usage data is what reveals the difference for your portfolio rather than a generic office standard applied everywhere. The payoff for employees is very tangible: More consistent access to the space type they actually need, when they need it Fewer overcrowded rooms and "ghosted" bookings competing for the same square footage A workplace that visibly adapts as team composition and work patterns change The confidence that a space was designed around how a team actually works, not a generic standard, shows up directly in experience scores. Real-life example: A scientific approach to neighborhood planning at Bread Financial Jason Finneran, who leads workplace strategy at Bread Financial, brought a more scientific approach to neighborhood planning and space design, using occupancy data in place of intuition-led layout decisions. The shift let his team assess employee needs directly instead of guessing at them, and adjust space design as those needs shifted over time. That's the practical version of a data-driven design strategy: a standing process for matching space to how your people really work. The Role of AI and Predictive Planning in Modern Design Strategy Static ratios assume the future looks like the past: same headcount, same attendance pattern, same team structure. AI-driven scenario modeling drops that assumption and instead asks what a proposed design will actually do once real people move through it. Predictive Planning, VergeSense's scenario-modeling capability and part of the Space Planning toolset, is built on the Large Spatial Model, trained on more than 250M+ sq ft of measured workplace data . That training set is what lets the model score a proposed layout against real behavioral patterns instead of a rule of thumb. Predictive Planning uses the LSM to run thousands of demand simulations against a proposed layout, scoring how it holds up under different attendance levels, headcount changes, and policy shifts. A design team can see where a plan will break (and where it holds) before construction crews arrive. Data-Driven Workplaces vs. Smart Offices It's worth drawing a quick distinction. A data-driven workplace uses occupancy and behavioral data to inform design and policy decisions. A smart office uses connected technology, badge readers, wayfinding apps, connected lighting, to make the day-to-day experience of being in the office easier. The two aren't competing categories. A smart office often runs on data-driven design underneath it, and a data-driven design strategy frequently ends up justifying the smart-office investments a team makes next. Tying Workplace Design Strategy to Measurable Outcomes None of this matters if it doesn't show up in the metrics leadership already tracks: utilization, space availability, cost avoidance, and employee experience signals. Utilization tells a team whether a space is earning its square footage. Space availability tells them whether employees can actually find the room type they need during the windows when demand peaks, not just on average. Cost avoidance, an expansion skipped, a lease renewal reconsidered, a build-out resized, is where design decisions show up on a CFO's radar, and experience signals, survey scores or complaints logged with facilities, round out the picture. A design strategy grounded in data gives each of those metrics a clear before-and-after. Utilization stops being a lagging annual number and becomes something a team can watch shift as a change rolls out. Real-life example: $13M in avoided expansion costs at a biotech company A biotechnology company's San Francisco headquarters looked full on paper, but occupancy data showed a large share of that space was held passively — by a bag, a jacket, or a laptop, rather than an employee actually working. The team created designated areas for personal belongings and freed up the space that had been sitting idle instead of signing off on a costly expansion. The change avoided $13M annually in expansion costs the company had been planning to make , without adding a single square foot. How to Get Started With a Data-Driven Design Strategy Initiating data-based workplace design strategies doesn't require a full sensor rollout on day one. Most teams begin with a single portfolio, establish a usage baseline, and use that data to make the next real design decision, whether that's a lease renewal, a redesign, or a policy change. From there, the strategy compounds. Each decision generates more usage data, which sharpens the next scenario model, which makes the next design call easier to defend in front of leadership. That's what Predictive Planning is built to do: turn every design decision into a testable scenario before it's built, and every measured outcome into signal for the next one. The result is a design strategy that gets sharper over time instead of stale and, on the CFO's side of the ledger, avoided expansions, resized build-outs, and lease renewals sized to actual demand rather than assumed headcount. Ready to see what a data-driven workplace design strategy looks like in your portfolio? See how VergeSense's Predictive Planning models space demand against real occupancy patterns — before you commit to a redesign, a lease decision, or a build-out. Book a Demo → FAQs About Workplace Design Strategy What Data Sources Feed a Data-Driven Workplace Design Strategy? Area sensors, WiFi infrastructure, videoconferencing data, and space-booking systems can all feed a design strategy. Area sensors offer the most granular view, measuring occupancy at the room and desk level, while WiFi data covers building- and floor-level trends. Most teams combine multiple sources rather than relying on just one. How Often Should a Workplace Design Strategy Be Reviewed? A workplace design strategy should be reviewed on a quarterly cadence for most portfolios, aligned with lease decisions and headcount changes. Continuously updated occupancy data means a team doesn't have to wait for a scheduled review to catch a shift, but a regular checkpoint keeps decisions tied to current behavior. Do You Need Sensors to Start a Data-Driven Design Strategy? No, you don't need sensors to start a data-driven design strategy. Predictive Planning can model how a floor plan will perform using a floor plan, headcount, and attendance policy alone. Sensors add continuously updated ground truth once a design is in place, but they aren't a prerequisite for the first scenario model. What's the Difference Between a Space Plan and a Workplace Design Strategy? A space plan is a single layout for a point in time. A workplace design strategy is the ongoing process, and the data behind it, for updating that layout as team composition, attendance, and space demand change.

body_text: July 15, 2026 16:05 ET SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO, Calif., July 15, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Surrozen, Inc. (“Surrozen” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: SRZN), a biotechnology company pioneering targeted therapeutics to harness the power of Wnt signaling to address the underlying drivers of disease in sight-threatening ophthalmic conditions, today announced that Company management will present at an upcoming healthcare investor conference. H.C. Wainwright 6 th Annual Ophthalmology Virtual Conference on Wednesday, July 22, 2026 Fireside Chat at 10:00 AM Pacific Time/1:00 PM Eastern Time Interested parties may access the audio webcast for the conference via the Investors section of the Surrozen website at https://investors.surrozen.com/events-presentations/events-calendar beginning at 1:00 PM Eastern Time on July 22, 2026. A replay of the webcast will be archived on the website www.surrozen.com for at least 30 days. About Surrozen Surrozen is a biotechnology company, pioneering a new class of Wnt-based therapeutics designed to harness the power of Wnt signaling to treat sight-threatening ophthalmic conditions. Built on deep scientific expertise and a proprietary antibody-engineering platform, Surrozen develops multifunctional biologics that selectively activate Wnt signaling in combination with other key disease pathways. Our approach aims to deliver best-in-class, durable therapies that have the potential to transform patient outcomes in some of the most pressing unmet medical needs in ocular diseases.
